output:
*Interview with Rosa Häfeli, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Sit down, Madame Häfeli. You are not in any trouble. I only want to hear about the evening, in your own way.

ROSA: Herrgott, Monsieur, I have never sat in a room with the police in it. I will stand, if it is the same to you. I have been in this house since I was a girl from the Emmental, and nobody has ever asked me into a room like this.

MATTHEY: Stand if you prefer. Tell me about the kitchen.

ROSA: My kitchen is at the back, and it is the best room in the house. The copper is always bright and the range draws. Tonight I had the champagne glasses out on the long table, all of Madame's good ones, and I polished every one twice. Madame would not forgive a smear on a glass at the New Year.

MATTHEY: And the clock on your wall?

ROSA: That is my American alarm clock. It is cheap, but it keeps good time for what it is. I keep it fast on purpose, so that nothing in this house is ever late. The bread, the soup, the master's tray. When the temple struck ten, my kitchen clock showed a quarter past ten. I keep it fast on purpose.

MATTHEY: Did Fräulein Lina come down to you?

ROSA: Fräulein Lina came down into the kitchen at twenty-three minutes to eleven by my kitchen clock, and she stayed with me until after the temple struck eleven. She is a quiet one. She sat by the range and we did the glasses together. She did not say much, and I did not ask her to. She is a good girl, and she was very upset, though she would not show it.

MATTHEY: And the house above you?

ROSA: We heard Madame's piano begin at twelve minutes to eleven by my kitchen clock, and stop at one minute past eleven by my kitchen clock. It was Chopin. Madame plays Chopin when she is thinking of something. I know the nocturnes so well I could hum you the one she played.

MATTHEY: Did you hear the hall clock?

ROSA: I heard the hall clock strike eleven when my kitchen clock showed three minutes past eleven. That is the old Morbier, the long-case one that strikes from its own face. Monsieur would never let anyone touch it, and he would never let anyone say a word against it either.

MATTHEY: Tell me about going upstairs.

ROSA: Madame had said the master would come down for the toast, and I was to fetch him, as I do every year. I went up the stairs to the atelier. The door was open. He was on the floor by his bench, and the brass mallet from the bench was lying there beside him. Oh, Herrgott. The regulator on the wall had stopped. His little repeater was in his hand, the one he spent four years on, and his hand was closed on it. I did not touch him. I went down the stairs as fast as my legs would take me.

MATTHEY: Whom did you tell?

ROSA: I told Madame. I could not say anything else for a while, and Madame did not ask me to.

MATTHEY: Take your time.

ROSA: Monsieur, I have nothing to hide, and still my hands are shaking. In my village the gendarme meant a bad thing, a man who came to take your cow or your son. I am frightened of you, and I am sorry for it, but I cannot help it. I am not a clever woman. I only know my kitchen and my copper and my clocks.

MATTHEY: You are doing well. Tell me only what you saw and heard, nothing more.

ROSA: That is all I have. Madame has been good to me, better than my own mother was. Whatever you need from me, you will have, but I will not say a thing about Madame that is not true. She is a proud woman, and she has had a hard year, and she is not one to cry in front of a policeman.

MATTHEY: Thank you, Madame Häfeli. You may go back to your kitchen.

ROSA: Thank you, Monsieur. Please, the glasses. I left them on the table, and no one has touched them since.
